notes.short: A saying: “a live dog is better than a dead lion”
notes.about: The verse sets a live dog beside a dead lion in a short saying read as a proverb. While a man lives there is still hope, and even the lowliest life is better than the greatest who has died.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: a live dog is better than a dead lion
figure.means: the lowliest person still alive is better off than the greatest who has died, for the living still have hope

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. Clarke supposes it was a proverb and explains it: the smallest measure of life is better than the largest of dead matter, and the poorest living peasant is infinitely above Alexander the Great.
notes.limit: The writers differ on where the saying began: one supposes it was already a proverb, the other lists it among sayings first found in Scripture that later passed into common use.

cites.quote: A living dog is better than a dead lion - I suppose this was a proverb. The smallest measure of animal existence is better than the largest of dead matter. The poorest living peasant is infinitely above Alexander the Great.

notes.short: A saying: dead flies spoil the perfumer's oil
notes.about: The verse opens with a picture: dead flies make the perfumer’s oil stink. It then applies it: a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. The picture is read as a saying first found here that has since passed into common use.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil
figure.means: a small thing can spoil something precious, as the verse says a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the opening words under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. The verse itself gives the application to a little folly.
notes.limit: Only one writer cited here calls the picture a proverb.

notes.short: Old age and death in one long picture
notes.about: The days of adversity in verse 1 are pictured: the lights grow dark, “the keepers of the house tremble”, the watchers at the windows see dimly, the almond tree blossoms. The writers read it as old age, the house as the failing body, and two of them read verse 6 as death.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the keepers of the house tremble
figure.means: the body failing in old age, pictured as a house whose keepers, strong men, grinders and watchers are the hands and arms, legs, teeth and eyes

notes.evidence: Poole calls verse 2 and the verses after it wholly allegorical. W. T. Bullock (Barnes' Notes) says the body in old age and death is pictured as a decaying house; Clarke, that the body is compared to a house; Henry, that old age is described in figurative expressions, and death in verse 6; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls verse 6 a double image of death, as verses 1 to 5 are of old age.
notes.limit: The writers differ on verse 6: one reads the silver cord and golden bowl as a hanging lamp whose cord and bowl answer to the spinal marrow and skull; another reads the cord as the bond between soul and body.

cites.quote: which seems not to agree with the context, partly because the dimness of their sight is expressed in the next verse, and partly because both his and the following verses are wholly allegorical. Or rather, 2. Figuratively, and that either, 1. Of the outward parts of the body, and especially of the face

The body in old age and death is here described under the figure of a decaying house with its inmates and furniture. This verse is best understood as referring to the change which old age brings to four parts of the body, the arms ("the keepers"), the legs ("the strong men"), the teeth ("the grinders"), and the eyes.

cites.quote: The Body of man is here compared to a House: - mark the metaphors and their propriety. 1. The keepers shall tremble - the hands become paralytic, as is constantly the case, less or more, in old age. 2. The strong men shall bow - The legs become feeble, and unable to support the weight of the body.

cites.quote: The decays and infirmities of old age are here elegantly described in figurative expressions … Then the keepers of the house tremble. The head, which is as the watch-tower, shakes, and the arms and hands … shake too … Death will … take down the earthly house of this tabernacle … the silver cord, by which soul and body were wonderfully fastened together

A double image to represent death, as in Ecc 12:1-5, old age: (1) A lamp of frail material, but gilded over, often in the East hung from roofs by a cord of silk and silver interwoven; as the lamp is dashed down and broken, when the cord breaks, so man at death; the golden bowl of the lamp answers to the skull … "the silver cord" is the spinal marrow
